entities.name: Alfonso de Valdés
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alfonso de Valdés (1490, Cuenca – October 3, 1532, Vienna) was a pivotal Spanish humanist and diplomat who served as secretary of Latin letters in the Imperial chancellery of Emperor Charles V. A key figure in the dissemination of Erasmian thought in Spain and at the heart of European power, Valdés was the twin brother of the equally influential Juan de Valdés. His intellectual output provided a sophisticated, if controversial, defense of Imperial policies during a period of intense religious and political upheaval, notably the Protestant Reformation and the Italian Wars. His direct access to the emperor and his command of humanist rhetoric positioned him uniquely to shape both policy and public perception.

Valdés's most significant contributions are his two polemical dialogues, "Diálogo de Lactancio y un Arcediano" (Dialogue of Lactantius and an Archdeacon, 1527) and "Diálogo de Mercurio y Carón" (Dialogue of Mercury and Charon, 1528). The former, published anonymously, offered an audacious justification for the Sack of Rome by Imperial troops in 1527, portraying it as divine punishment for the papacy's corruption and an unfortunate but necessary step towards church reform. The latter extended this critique, satirizing corrupt clergy and advocating for Erasmian ideals of spiritual renewal and peace. Beyond his literary endeavors, Valdés was actively involved in diplomatic missions, including negotiations with Pope Clement VII, leveraging his intellectual prowess to advance Imperial interests and the cause of religious concord.
